newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: COSTELLO PROPOSES SIMPLIFYING WHOLESALE TAX, RATHER THAN GST
The Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says he will consider simplifying the wholesale tax system rather than introducing a consumption tax.
In an interview on commercial radio, Mr Costello would not directly say he personally supported a GST, instead saying the indirect tax-base needed to be broadened.
But he did indicate a flattening of wholesale tax rates may be a viable option.
Mr Costello says wholesale tax rates could be simplified by having one rate, applying to a broader range of goods.
The Treasurer says the advantage of such a move would be avoiding classification problems, which he says is a huge problem with the system at the moment.
NAB CHIEF CHALLENGES COSTELLO'S OPTIMISM
One of Australia's top bankers has challenged the Federal Treasurer's optimism about the economy.
Peter Costello yesterday forecast stronger economic growth, in the wake of good figures on retail and construction, and suggestions of a lift in Australia's credit rating.
But the Managing Director of the National Australia Bank, Don Argus, says business confidence remains subdued.

Mr Argus: "The business community is at the coalface, and they understand that it is probably not moving as quickly yet as what we'd like to see. In fact, you'll see this afternoon we put out the results of our quarterly survey, and it's still relatively flat.
Mr Argus says while there is some movement, things perhaps are not moving as quickly as Mr Costello would like.
TRIALS OF LODGING TAX RETURNS VIA THE INTERNET UNDERWAY
Trials are under way which look like leading to Australians lodging their tax returns over the internet.
Tax Commissioner Michael Carmody says 2,000 volunteers are taking part in a pilot project this year, and believes that next year there will be a version of Tax Pack on the world-wide web.
In Brisbane, Mr Carmody said they are working on the privacy and security issues.
Mr Carmody says those issues are the reason why lodging tax returns over the internet is not happening now.
However, he says there have been developments in security, and adds the Tax Office is confident that by next year, security won't be an issue.
PRISON OFFICERS CALL FOR NATIONAL CODE TO REDUCE DEATHS
Prison officers have called for a national code of practice and training to reduce indigenous deaths in custody.
A report prepared by prison officers and Aboriginal members of the Public Sector Union recommends all officers receive training in risk assessment, crisis management and indigenous issues.
Senior Victorian Prison Officer, John Dixon, says members have told him they may have saved Aboriginal lives if they had been trained to recognise suicidal behaviour.
Mr Dixon says bad prison adminstration is responsible for many indigenous deaths in custody.
He says in Western Australia, it is not unusal for an indigneous prisoner to be sentenced in Perth and sent to Broome by road, which takes three days.
Mr Dixon says often when the prisoner gets to Broome Prison, he is told he after staying one night he must be transported back to Perth again to answer further charges.
Mr Dixon says such a failing in Western Australia's classification system places immense stress on Aboriginal prisoners in that State.
FEARS NEWCASTLE COULD LOSE FRIGATES WORK
A split in the Transfield Holdings Group, which is building 10 ANZAC frigates for the Australian and New Zealand Navies, could see Newcastle lose its share of the work.
Transfield has broken up into two separate groups; Transfield Construction and Transfield Defence Systems.

The Metalworkers Union says Transfield in Newcastle has built modules for the first five frigates, but will now have to bid for the rest of the work against Transfield Defence Systems. Transfield's Liam Bathgate says the company will take into account Newcastle's four-year involvement in the project, and the expectation that it would continue to be involved for the term of the contract.

Mr Bathgate says while the company will take account of the skills and enthusiasm of people in the area to do the work, its decision will be based largely on competitiveness and conformity with the contract requirements.
TERRITORY GETS ADVICE ON EUTHANASIA BILL
The Northern Territory's Attorney-General has received legal opinions on a private member's pro-voluntary euthanasia bill.
Federal legislation prohibits the territories from passing laws legalising voluntary euthanasia.
So the Member for Wanguri, John Bailey, tabled a bill in May providing for a $50 fine for those involved in the process, who have followed strict guidelines.
Attorney-General Denis Burke has sought legal opinion on the bill's chances of surviving a High Court challenge.
He has now received those opinions, but won't say when they'll be distributed to members of parliament.
Mr Bailey says he understands the advice is divided - one opinion saying his bill would stand up to a challenge, another saying it would have difficulties, and a third has an each way bet.
ASTHMA PUFFERS MAY INCREASE CATARACT RISK
An Australian eye study has revealed that steroid puffers used to control asthma and emphysema, may increase the risk of cataracts.
The findings, published in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine, researched people with severe asthma aged over 49.
The findings don't relate to the common blue ventalin puffer.
One of the authors, professor Stephen Leeder from the University of Sydney, says it had been thought that the small doses of steroids would not affect the eye.
"It's a trade-off between the small risk associated with their use, and the benefit that can be gained from their use for asthma," Professor Leeder said.
He says the aim is appropriate treatment, which means prescribing enough to keep the asthma under control without excessive use of the puffers.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
